units.name: 31 More Than a Game
units.passage: For a long time in sports, a referee's decision was final. Fans might shout and players might argue, but nothing changed, and the match simply went on. Then, several decades ago, instant replay arrived. Coaches could now question a call and request that the officials look at the video again. Games became fairer, but they also took longer. Today, a growing number of professional leagues are turning to another kind of technology: automated referee systems. These machines get calls right every single time, and they cut down on the long pauses caused by reviews. Human referees are still needed for difficult judgments, such as charging in basketball and pass interference in football. Even so, leagues expect automated systems to make games both fairer and quicker. Tennis already shows how well this can work. Sony's Hawk-Eye Live system can tell exactly where a ball hits the court. It has become so trustworthy that it now makes every line call at the U.S. Open.

units.name: 32 Copying Routines
units.passage: People tend to imitate those who seem more successful than they are. Fortunately for them, plenty of CEOs, celebrities, and influencers post their daily routines online. These stars often claim that such habits keep them productive and help them stay on top. Mark Wahlberg gets up at 2:30 in the morning, and Elon Musk splits his day into blocks of five minutes. For most ordinary people, routines like these are simply too difficult. Why, then, do successful people stick to them? The main reason is psychological. Their success relies on things beyond their control, such as the stock market or trends on social media. Daily routines, however, are something they can choose and manage by themselves, so these habits give them a feeling of control. Even though the habits are not always sensible, they believe that keeping them will help them stay successful. Another reason is that money gradually loses its thrill. Surrounded by other successful people, they may stop feeling special. So they invent extreme routines that few people could follow, and doing this makes them feel better than others.

units.name: 33 AI, It’s Everywhere
units.passage: Red squirrels are the only squirrel species that is native to the UK. However, their survival has been at risk ever since grey squirrels were brought over from North America near the end of the 1800s. Rich people kept (a) them as pets, and because people found (b) them attractive, some were set free in large gardens and parks. Today, greys outnumber reds by over 2 million. (c) Greys are larger, eat more, and use up more space, so the number of red squirrels has fallen quickly. To protect (d) the reds, scientists have turned to artificial intelligence (AI). A system named Squirrel Agent can distinguish between the two kinds by looking at their size, shape, and other features. It operates special feeders that open only for red squirrels and keep (e) grey ones away. This, however, is only the first step. Someday, the AI may be able to recognize not just each species but also each individual squirrel. By following families and gathering data, it could protect red squirrels over a long period.

units.name: 34 Skin Science
units.passage: Our skin is always producing new cells, so why don't scars and tattoos disappear? The answer has to do with collagen and ink particles. Our skin is made up mostly of collagen, a protein that fibroblast cells produce. When skin gets hurt, new fibroblasts make a special kind of collagen called scar collagen, which is not the same as normal collagen. Although the skin cells keep renewing themselves, this scar collagen does not go away. Interestingly, the skin of an unborn baby can recover from injuries without leaving scars. This is because it makes fetal collagen, which differs from the collagen in adults. If scientists discovered how to make adult skin produce fetal collagen, people might one day heal from wounds with no scars at all. Tattoos, however, stay for a different reason: their ink particles are too big for white blood cells to clear away. Tattoo removal lasers, which can be very painful, solve this problem by breaking the ink into very small pieces like dust. This lets white blood cells carry the pieces out of the skin, so the tattoo slowly fades.

units.name: 35 A Win-Win Solution
units.passage: Snow leopards are hunters that live in the mountains of 12 countries in Asia. These big cats are rare, and they are officially listed as a vulnerable species. Recently, the wild animals that snow leopards hunt in the Himalayas have become fewer, so the leopards often attack farm animals instead. This makes the leopards' conflict with the local people even worse, because villagers want to kill the leopards to protect their animals. To help both sides live together, a simple plan was created. A trekking program was developed so that tourists could look for snow leopards in the wild. Local people received help in opening places for visitors to stay, and they were trained to work as guides. The plan has worked well. Studies show that getting locals involved in tourism has made them feel more positive about all wild animals, including snow leopards. In areas where leopards used to kill many farm animals, local people now make ten times more money from tourism than they once made from raising livestock.

units.name: 36 Tiny but Amazing
units.passage: Bacteria do a lot of good for us. They help produce food and fuel, and they break down waste. Surprisingly, they might also help bring rain! Certain bacteria, known as ice-nucleation active bacteria, carry special proteins that allow water to freeze at higher temperatures than usual. On the ground, these bacteria can harm crops by causing frost. But when they are carried up into the sky, they create ice crystals, and these crystals can turn into rain or snow. Some scientists believe that humans may already be affecting rainfall, because huge fields of crops send these bacteria into the air. A few experts even suggest growing particular plants to make more rain. This idea, however, has some problems. Farmers may not want to put their crops in danger. Also, if a cloud holds too many bacteria, it might not produce any rain at all. On top of that, deciding who creates rain and where it should fall could cause serious arguments between neighboring countries. Bacteria may be helpful, but completely controlling rain is still a difficult task.

units.name: 37 Word of the Year
units.passage: In 2024, Oxford University Press named "brain rot" its word of the year. The expression describes how a person's mind and thinking ability can get worse when someone spends too many hours on shallow or meaningless material online, like short-form videos. People usually say it lightly, as a kind of joke. But could the phrase be more accurate than we think? A lot of people say they feel worn out in the head after watching short clips for hours at a time. Recent studies by researchers have also shown that online content can lower concentration, weaken attention, and harm memory. These effects become even more serious for young people whose brains are still developing, especially when they are exposed to a lot of online content and often do several tasks at once. So "brain rot" may look like a trendy word that will soon disappear, but it might actually point to a real thinking problem of the digital era.

units.name: 38 A Scientist’s Puzzle
units.passage: For many years, scientists believed that a species which had been around for a long time had a better chance of surviving into the future. In their view, a long history showed that a species was strong. In the early 1970s, a scientist named Van Valen tried to show that this popular idea was correct. However, he failed, because the numbers simply did not match it. He started to ask himself if evolution was so harsh and cruel that species with long histories had only been fortunate. This new explanation matched the data much better. In fact, old species and young species faced about the same risk of dying out. Some species may survive for a very long time by luck, but their chances do not improve as time passes. The reason is that competition in evolution is not like a soccer match, where the winning team can rest after the game. In nature, the struggle to survive never ends, and no victory is permanent.

units.name: 39 The Power of Innovation
units.passage: Kites are more than toys. They can also be very practical tools of technology. Science has used kites for a long time, from Benjamin Franklin's experiments with lightning to the first cable that was carried across Niagara Falls. Today, SkySails, a company from Germany, has developed a system that uses a kite to pull ships across the sea. The company tried it out on a boat, and it was successful. According to its CEO, the system may lower fuel use by at least 30 percent, which would save money as the price of oil goes up. Long ago, big sailing ships depended on the wind, but steering them was not easy. Steam engines were simpler to handle, yet combining sails and steam created new trouble. Running both at the same time was hard, and the ships became less efficient. SkySails solves this by taking away the mast and flying a kite tied to the ship with a strong cable. As a result, ships become steadier and use energy better. Can a kite truly move giant ships across the ocean? Only the wind can answer that.

units.name: 40 Baby Animals
units.passage: Baby animals are extremely delicate. A bird embryo will die if its eggshell cracks, and young shellfish cannot live unless they discover just the right place in the ocean. At the same time, baby animals can be powerful enough to change the world around them. Some young insects, known to farmers as pests, can ruin whole fields of crops, and the larvae of certain beetles are even able to eat plastic. Human babies also have this combination of weakness and strength. At birth, we have no idea what words mean. Yet we want to learn so badly that we can absorb several languages simply by listening to them, which grown-ups find hard to do. Babies also have weak immune systems, so they catch infections that rarely make adults sick. However, these immature immune systems are built to cooperate with helpful bacteria, and this finally lets babies become strong and healthy. Being very young may look like a disadvantage, but under the right conditions, it can turn into a big benefit.

units.name: 41 Crisis Escape No.1
units.passage: Imagine you are in an elevator that is falling. Could jumping at the very last second save your life? Probably not, since a jump hardly lowers the force of the crash. A falling elevator speeds up as gravity pulls it toward the ground. Because you are dropping just as fast as the elevator, you feel weightless for a moment, so it is almost impossible to push off the floor. It is also very hard to choose exactly the right moment to jump. And even if you succeed in jumping at the perfect time, the speed you gain going up is tiny next to the speed of the falling elevator, so it does little to soften the crash. Instead, your best chance of staying alive is to lie down flat on your back. Lying this way spreads the force of the crash across your whole body, which lowers the pressure on any one part and reduces the chance of a serious injury. Luckily, today's elevators come with several safety devices, like automatic brakes and extra cables, so a complete free fall almost never happens.

units.name: 42 Everyday Sustainability
units.passage: A carbon label is an easy way of showing the carbon footprint of a meal or a food item, so shoppers can see how it affects the environment. A carbon footprint means the whole amount of greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide (CO₂), that are released while a product is made, moved, and used, or while an activity is carried out. Because these labels measure and show how much carbon and other greenhouse gases are released, they make people more aware of sustainability. With carbon labels, food makers can develop meals that produce less carbon, and restaurants can help diners choose dishes that are better for the planet based on clear information. In this way, labels encourage both businesses and customers to act in greener ways. Some shoppers might not pay attention to the labels, but many experts think labeling can still lead to good results. Even small changes in what we eat can lower total greenhouse gas emissions. As more people learn about their effect on the environment, carbon labels will become even more useful for supporting sustainability.

units.name: 43 Communication Isn’t Easy
units.passage: Talks between people do not always run smoothly, and they often drift away from the subject. One helpful way to deal with this is called a content-to-process shift. In this method, you stop focusing on the off-topic subject, which is the content, and start paying attention to how the talk itself is going, which is the process. For instance, you might say, "It seems we have moved on to old events instead of the issue we wanted to discuss." A comment like this can guide everyone back to the main point. This method also lets you share how you feel about the conversation. You could say, "I'm happy that we are getting somewhere with this problem. We are truly understanding each other!" The shift is particularly helpful when people become emotional and start to speak loudly. In that kind of situation, you might say, "I notice that both of us are becoming a bit upset. This topic is obviously a delicate one." Words like these can help calm things down. The important thing is to use a neutral, relaxed tone, so your words do not feel like an attack.

units.name: 44 Hypnosis
units.passage: Many people believe that hypnosis can uncover memories hidden deep in the mind, but this is not true. People under hypnosis are easily affected by others, so they may "remember" things that never happened, shaped by the hypnotist's words or by their own imagination. Even if hypnosis brings memories back, they are not always accurate. For instance, a crime victim under hypnosis might describe a suspect's tattoo with great confidence, and the description could still be wrong. On the other hand, hypnosis has shown real value in medicine. Doctors use it to ease pain, stress, and worry, and it helps patients receiving chemotherapy deal with nausea. Sometimes it has even worked as a kind of anesthesia during surgery, so an operation can be done without the usual painkillers. Some psychologists also use hypnosis to help people quit bad habits like biting their nails or to build their confidence. So, hypnosis may not work well for its most famous purpose, but it offers useful medical and psychological benefits that make people's lives better in many ways.

units.name: 45 Nature’s Triggers
units.passage: When people study what causes earthquakes, they usually search beneath the ground first, because that seems like the obvious place for an answer. Recent research, however, tells us to look up at the sky as well. In 2020, northern Japan began to experience a new series of earthquakes that kept repeating, unlike the occasional quakes the area had before. Scientists at MIT wanted to know whether something besides ground movement was behind this new pattern. They discovered a close connection between the recent quakes and extreme weather. When heavy rain and snow soak into the ground, the water fills small gaps in the rocks below. This raises the pressure deep inside the Earth, so the ground can slip more easily, even without much force. Because of this, earthquakes may occur more often or sooner than expected. What matters even more is that heavy rain and snow are linked to climate change. Higher temperatures allow more moisture to gather in the air, which produces heavier rain and snow. If such extreme weather continues, it could have a big effect on earthquakes all over the world.

units.name: 46 Beyond Fun
units.passage: Today, many video games offer detailed stories and beautiful graphics. Starting a modern game can feel like walking into a completely different world. What is more, this world is often full of real history, traditions, and cultural tales, so players can experience other societies and lifestyles. In Assassin's Creed, for instance, players can look closely at the clothes, customs, and myths of past civilizations, from feudal Japan to ancient Egypt. Animal Crossing includes real festivals as events in the game, like Japan's Tanabata Star Festival and the Lunar New Year. In the same way, Roblox has a wide range of experiences made by its users. They present various cultures through things such as virtual historical places and global festivals held online. These cultural elements make playing a game richer, and they also help players understand cultures different from their own. As a result, gamers can grow to feel empathy for people from other cultures and to respect them.

units.name: 47 Animal Signals
units.passage: Many animals find it easier to tell where a high-pitched sound is coming from than a low-pitched one. However, high-frequency sounds have a serious weakness. Their energy fades fast, and leaves, grass, and branches easily scatter them or bounce them back. For this reason, ultrasonic calls, which are too high for people to hear, cannot go very far. The low song of a blue whale can travel across a whole ocean, while the ultrasonic song of a singing mouse reaches only animals close by. On top of that, ultrasound vanishes very quickly. This could be why only a small number of mammals, such as mice, dolphins, and small bats, are known to use it. Still, this short range can be useful, because it controls who gets to hear the sound. A baby mouse, for example, can call to its parent without letting predators know. So ultrasound can be used for secret communication, not only because humans cannot hear it but also because it does not travel far. There may be more animals using ultrasound than we think.

units.name: 48 Meet the Minions!
units.passage: Ever since the animated film Despicable Me came out in theaters, the cute yellow Minions have won the love of many people. But the more we like these warm and funny characters, the more curious we become about what they are saying. What special words and expressions do they use in the films? People say that the directors made up the Minion language by borrowing words and expressions from a variety of languages. Fans have looked closely at Minion words to discover which languages were used, and they have learned that many words come from Hindi, English, and Korean. For instance, "Tank you" clearly comes from the English "thank you." Minions also count to three in Korean, saying "Hana, Dul, Sae." In addition, they use lots of words for food, since they obviously love eating! They mention "poulet tikka masala," which combines "poulet," the French word for chicken, with "tikka masala," a spicy dish from India. They also talk about "gelato," the Italian word for ice cream.

units.name: 49 Facts You Don’t See
units.passage: Have you ever shut one eye while trying to hit a faraway target, for example in archery or when firing a pistol? If so, there is a scientific reason behind this habit, and it is called binocular rivalry. Normally, our two eyes send the brain slightly different pictures, and the brain joins them into one clear view. But sometimes the picture from the left eye does not match the picture from the right eye. When that happens, the two images do not blend together. Instead, they compete, and each one tries to win over the other. Imagine that your left eye sees nothing but up-and-down lines while your right eye sees only side-to-side lines. You might expect to see a neat grid of crosses, but you will not. Rather, you notice patches of vertical lines here and patches of horizontal lines there, partly mixed together. Some people can hold back one of the competing images and focus on the other. Others cannot do this well, so they shut one eye. They keep the dominant eye open because it usually sees more clearly than the weaker one.

units.name: 50 How to Express?
units.passage: Sugar is a sweet material that we add to cakes, cookies, pies, and candy to make them delicious. It can also hide the bitter taste of medicine so that patients can get it down more easily. For this reason, companies that produced pills started covering them with a hard shell of sugar. These days, the word sugarcoat has two meanings. It can describe an actual coat of sugar, but it can also describe a particular way of telling people news. When you sugarcoat something, you present it as nicer or more acceptable than it truly is, so the hard truth feels softer. In other words, you are not completely honest and direct; you leave out some of the painful or negative parts. Imagine a sports team that ended its spring season at the very bottom of the rankings. Rather than admitting, "We played terribly," the coach might say, "We had some difficulties this season, but we are already trying to get better."

units.name: 51 Back to the Past
units.passage: In an age full of advanced technology, a surprising number of young people are choosing older and simpler gadgets, such as disposable cameras. Since 2019, sales of these cameras have been rising, and much of the demand comes from Gen Z. Most of them were born after the 1990s, when disposable cameras were first at their most popular. So why are they attracted to such a basic device? First, the pictures it produces look a little rough and warm. They are not perfect like digital photos, but they feel honest and real. Second, you cannot check or change your pictures after taking them. Because of this, every click of the button seems more meaningful, and you pay closer attention to the moment in front of you. It is a bit ironic: the photos stored on our phones are the ones that seem easy to throw away, while prints from a disposable camera seem to last forever. And how wonderful is it to hold a picture that looks exactly like the ones your parents took in their youth?

units.name: 52 This or That?
units.passage: Should a tomato be called a fruit or a vegetable? People have argued about this for hundreds of years. Scientifically speaking, a tomato is a fruit, but in 1893 the U.S. Supreme Court reached a different decision. The case started because of money. At that time, imported vegetables were taxed at 10 percent, but imported fruits were not taxed at all. John Nix, who brought fruit into New York from abroad, argued that he should not have to pay any tax on his tomatoes. Justice Horace Gray, however, explained that while tomatoes are fruits to scientists, most people use them like vegetables in everyday meals. They are eaten with main dishes and in salads, not as sweet desserts. For this reason, the court decided that tomatoes were vegetables, and Nix was required to pay the tax. Still, the argument has not ended. Tennessee and Ohio have both named the tomato their official state fruit, but New Jersey treats it as a vegetable and points to the court's decision. Fruit or vegetable, the tomato remains one of the world's great puzzles.

units.name: 53 The Corn Secret
units.passage: Long ago, the native people of Mexico found a clever way to prepare corn. They soaked it in water mixed with lime, which made the corn softer and much easier to grind. However, this method did something even more important. It allowed the body to take in niacin, also known as vitamin B3, a nutrient that is hidden inside corn. People who do not get enough niacin can suffer from a disease called pellagra, which may kill them if it is not treated in the right way. Thanks to their traditional cooking method, native Mexicans were protected from this illness without even knowing it. Later, Europeans carried corn to other parts of the world, but they did not learn the lime water technique. As a result, pellagra became common, particularly among poor families whose diet depended mainly on corn. Scientists needed centuries to discover the cause. This story teaches us that processing food is not always harmful. In some cases, it quietly helps us, changing plain foods into meals that keep people healthy and alive.

units.name: 54 Reach for Space
units.passage: The asteroid belt in our Solar System holds large amounts of precious metals, such as iron, nickel, gold, and platinum. Many people think it may also contain rare earth metals, which are necessary for making high-tech products. Companies in many countries are getting ready to dig up these resources in what some call a "new gold rush." However, space mining means more than the gold rushes of earlier times, when people only wanted to become rich. As technology keeps advancing, we need more and more rare earth elements. Unfortunately, digging them out of the ground on Earth damages the natural environment, and workers often have to labor in poisonous surroundings. If we move this industry into space, we can protect our planet's nature. Also, robots will do the actual mining, so people will not need to take on risky jobs anymore. Rather than hurting Earth, we can look to space as a smarter choice. Picture a future in which Earth remains a peaceful, unspoiled garden within the Solar System.

units.name: 55 Capital City Design
units.passage: Most nations run their government from a single capital, but a few have decided to use more than one. Rather than gathering every government office in one city, this approach stops any single region from gaining too much power, and it lets different parts of the country take part. South Africa, for example, has three capitals, and each one has its own job: Pretoria is home to the president, Cape Town is where lawmakers meet, and Bloemfontein holds the top court, where judges make major legal decisions. Malaysia took a different step. It moved many of its government offices to a new city called Putrajaya. The goal was to ease crowding in Kuala Lumpur, which is still the nation's center for money and culture. Cases like these show that more than one capital can bring real benefits. Power is balanced, conflicts between regions can shrink, and people feel that they are treated more fairly. One capital may be easier to manage, but a carefully planned system can keep a country stable for years to come. In some cases, spreading national power among regions is the wisest way to rule.

units.name: 56 Thought, The Quiet Activity
units.passage: Many people believe that when they think, a stream of words runs through their heads. But if you pause and really pay attention to your thoughts, you may notice that they seem messy and broken into pieces. The voice inside us usually gives us bits of words and short phrases, not neat, perfectly clear sentences. Language can show part of what our minds produce, but it is not the same as thinking. Consider a fast-paced video game. Players might yell short things such as "Oh no!" or "Got you!" as they react in a split second. If they needed to put every thought into spoken words, they would move as slowly as a snail. This shows that we are able to think without words, and in fact we do it constantly. There is more evidence. Some people have aphasia, a condition that makes language hard to use and is often caused by a stroke. Even so, many of them can still solve math problems or work through puzzles, as long as the tasks do not require words.

units.name: 57 Why Is Switzerland Special?
units.passage: More than 600 years ago, a Swiss holy man named Saint Nicholas of Flüe gave a simple piece of advice: "Stay out of other people's business." Even today, his words sum up the way Switzerland deals with other nations. The country is well known for being neutral. This means it refuses to support either side when other countries go to war, and it never sends its troops to join their battles. A few other nations in Europe, such as Austria, Finland, Ireland, and Sweden, follow a similar policy. However, Switzerland was the first to choose neutrality, and it remains the most famous example. Being neutral does not mean being weak, though. Switzerland keeps a powerful army that many people respect. Its soldiers train to protect their homeland from danger, and they also help keep peace in other parts of the world. Surprisingly, compared with its population, Switzerland has one of the biggest armies on Earth. The reason is that every healthy Swiss man receives military training and can be called on to serve in a national emergency. As a result, the country is always prepared for a crisis.

units.name: 58 You Are What You Eat
units.passage: What you eat, which is called nutrition, has a direct connection to your health. However, the order of the foods on your plate also matters. When people are free to decide what to eat, the order of eating can change the way their body functions. Most of these changes happen during the postprandial state, the time right after a meal when the body breaks down food and takes in nutrients. In this period, the kinds of food we eat and the order we eat them in have a strong effect on our blood sugar. For instance, foods rich in carbohydrates, such as white rice or bread, usually make blood sugar go up quickly, especially if we eat them at the start of a meal. Over time, this may cause long-term illnesses like diabetes. Research has found a different pattern when people begin their meals with vegetables and protein instead of carbohydrates. Their blood sugar tends to react differently. In fact, this way of eating is linked to a gentler increase in blood sugar, and people also feel full for longer.

units.name: 59 Good Products
units.passage: Inclusive design, also called universal design, means creating products that serve everyone well, including people with special needs. The name makes sense because such products can help all users. In everyday life, we often notice that features first made to support people with disabilities end up being used by many different people. For example, big letters with strong contrast are easier to read for people whose eyesight is poor. At the same time, they are helpful for anyone reading in low light or trying to read fast. Tools that can be adjusted, such as desks that move up and down or screens that users can set up their own way, make work easier for wheelchair users and for other office workers as well. Voice recognition is another example. Today it is a basic feature of phones and of virtual assistants such as Siri, and it is used by far more people than just those with vision problems. When designers think about the various needs of different users, they can make products that are better, smarter, and more useful. After all, accessibility is not only for a small group of people.

units.name: 60 Seeing the Invisible
units.passage: When we try to understand ideas that are abstract, we usually connect them to things that are concrete. In the case of time, most people use space as the concrete thing they compare it with. Research shows that people around the world picture time as if it were a kind of space. This is the reason we talk about the past as being behind us and the future as lying in front of us. It feels as though we are traveling away from yesterday and heading toward tomorrow. Thinking of time in this spatial way makes it easier to solve problems about time. Suppose you had breakfast before you walked the dog but after you read the newspaper. By placing these events along a line in your head, you can easily figure out which one came first. Metaphors like this are a useful tool for making abstract ideas easier to understand. By connecting things we can see with things we cannot see, we can use our strong visual thinking skills to make sense of time and other abstract ideas.
